source: Gick and Holyoak (1983) Schema induction and analogical transfer
finding: With no hint, a story analog is rarely used on a far target problem. Hinting to use it lifts success a lot. The gap is a noticing failure, not a failure to apply.
numbers: Radiation problem: about 30% gave the convergence solution after memorising the military story with no hint, about 75% with a hint; no-analog control under 10% (base rate assumed 10% from earlier replications). Authors: only a third or less of those who could use the analogy noticed it.
quote: only about 30% of our subjects produced the convergence solution, as opposed to about 75% who produced it when a hint was given
limits: Student samples, one story-problem family. The 10% base rate is assumed, not rerun.
agent_relevance: Retrieval of the right lesson is the bottleneck, not use of it. O7 needs an explicit step that asks which stored lesson might apply, not spontaneous recall.

source: Gick and Holyoak (1983) Schema induction and analogical transfer (Exp 1, cord problem)
finding: Same noticing gap with a second target problem (Maier cord problem), so it is not specific to the radiation problem.
numbers: High school classes, N=69 (25 analog-recall, 24 analog-summary, 20 control). Pendulum solution before hint: analog groups 71% vs control 20%. Total with hint: 98% vs 30%. Recall vs summary did not differ (68 vs 75% before hint).
limits: Booklet format, high school students. Control base rate here (20 to 39%) is far above the radiation problem's 10%, so the gain depends on how hard the target is.
agent_relevance: Easy-to-find solutions show smaller transfer gains. Lesson reuse should matter most on hard, rarely solved tasks.

source: Gick and Holyoak (1983) Schema induction and analogical transfer (Exp 2, verbal principle)
finding: Adding an abstract principle sentence to a single story did not help. The principle alone gave a moderate result.
numbers: Analog plus principle: about 30% before hint, about 80% total, virtually the same as analog only. Principle-only total 66%. All three conditions beat the 10% base rate before the hint. 28 of 31 subjects recalled part of the principle.
limits: The principle was read incidentally during a story-recall task. Authors say it could help in an explicit problem-solving context.
agent_relevance: A rule stored next to one example may not form a usable schema. One case plus a rule is not enough by itself.

source: Gick and Holyoak (1983) Schema induction and analogical transfer (Exp 3, diagram)
finding: A diagram of the solution did not help spontaneous noticing. The information in memory was enough but was never noticed.
numbers: Both analog conditions combined: 31% convergence solution before hint. Diagram-only: 1 of 15 (7%) before hint, 67% in total after hint, vs 78% for analog conditions.
limits: Small cells (n=15 in the diagram group).
agent_relevance: How a stored lesson is formatted does not fix the retrieval problem.

source: Gick and Holyoak (1983) Schema induction and analogical transfer (Exp 4, two analogs)
finding: Two analogs beat one. Quality of the schema the person writes predicts transfer.
numbers: N=98 (28 two similar analogs, 23 two dissimilar, 47 one analog plus an irrelevant story). Before hint: 45% two-analog vs 21% one-analog (G2=6.35, p<.01). Total: 80% vs 53%. Similar vs dissimilar pair: 39 vs 52% before hint, ns. Schema scored good 21%, intermediate 20%, poor 59%. Good schema: 91% solved before hint. Poor schema: 30% before hint, 70% total.
limits: Schema scoring done by the authors. Some cells are small.
agent_relevance: Comparing two solved cases and writing the shared structure is a concrete operator for lesson abstraction. Store the abstract schema, not only the cases.

source: Gick and Holyoak (1983) Schema induction and analogical transfer (Exp 5-6, principle and diagrams with two analogs)
finding: Once two analogs are compared, a stated principle and a diagram both raise transfer. Highlighting only helps when there is something to compare.
numbers: Exp 5: with principle 62% vs without 40% before hint (G2=6.75, p<.01); total 82% vs 67%. Good schemas 44% vs 10%. Exp 6, N=189: diagram 57% vs 37% before hint, total 92% vs 79%. Dissimilar analogs with diagrams gave 65% good schemas vs 44% for similar, but overall transfer did not differ.
limits: University students, one problem family.
agent_relevance: Order matters: compare at least two prior cases first, then state a rule. Matches a design where O7 abstracts from several cases.

source: Melby-Lervag, Redick and Hulme (2016) Working memory training does not improve performance on measures of intelligence or other measures of far transfer
finding: Large meta-analysis of working memory training. Near transfer is large. Far transfer is null once the control group is active.
numbers: 87 publications, 145 comparisons, Hedges g. Immediate near transfer g=0.80 [0.62,0.97] with treated controls, 1.88 with untreated. Far, treated controls: nonverbal ability 0.05 [-0.02,0.13] (k=67); verbal ability 0.05; word decoding 0.08; reading comprehension 0.15 (0.08 after excluding control declines); arithmetic 0.06. Untreated controls: nonverbal 0.20 (k=53).
quote: no evidence that working memory training yields improvements in so-called far-transfer abilities
limits: Treated vs untreated for nonverbal ability Q(1)=6.09, p=.01. Au et al. (2016) argued for g=0.13 on fluid intelligence in an earlier set.
agent_relevance: Training a general skill and hoping it spreads is the weak design. Gains against passive baselines can be expectation effects, so test the agent against an active baseline.

source: Melby-Lervag, Redick and Hulme (2016) Working memory training does not improve performance on measures of intelligence or other measures of far transfer (moderators and bias)
finding: Small, weak studies carry the far-transfer effect. Gain on the trained construct did not predict far gains. P-curve shows publication bias for treated-control studies.
numbers: Treated controls, groups of 20 or more: k=34, g=0.01. Groups under 20: k=25, g=0.26. Mediation: nonverbal ability vs near-transfer WM beta=-.01, p=.86 (k=26). P-curve treated controls z(11)=-2.19, flat or left-skewed. About 5-month follow-up: nonverbal ability g=-0.05 (k=12).
limits: Few follow-up studies for verbal outcomes (k=1 to 3).
agent_relevance: Inflated transfer claims come from small noisy tests. Evaluate lesson transfer on large item sets and report delayed tests.

source: Sala and Gobet (2017) Does far transfer exist? Negative evidence from chess, music, and working memory training
finding: Pooled effects of chess, music and working memory training on broader skills look small to moderate, but shrink with better control groups.
numbers: Overall: chess 0.34 [0.24,0.44]; music 0.16 [0.09,0.22]; WM training 0.12 [0.06,0.18]. Music: passive control 0.25 (k=64) vs active control 0.03 [-0.07,0.12] (k=54). WM: passive 0.18 vs active 0.05. Chess: only one study had an active control (0.10). WM training near transfer to other memory tasks 0.44 (active) and 0.46 (passive).
limits: Children and young adolescents; authors say older adults may differ. Chess evidence is mostly passive-control. Five meta-analyses pooled in a short summary article.
agent_relevance: Effect size falls as design quality rises. Use active controls (same prompt length, same token budget) when testing lesson reuse.

source: Sala and Gobet (2017) Does far transfer exist? Negative evidence from chess, music, and working memory training (correlational context)
finding: Chess and music experts outperform others by about half an SD, but training studies do not show that training causes the broader gain. Selection explains the correlation.
numbers: Chess players outperform non-players by about 0.5 SD in cognitive ability; the best-design training study gives about 0.10 SD.
limits: Same article; the correlational meta-analyses are only summarised.
agent_relevance: Do not read the good performance of a specialised agent as proof that its specialty transfers.

source: Barnett and Ceci (2002) When and where do we apply what we learn? A taxonomy for far transfer
finding: Debate on far transfer stalled because studies differ on many dimensions. A single far-transfer effect size is misguided. The paper proposes a 9-dimension framework (content and context dimensions such as knowledge domain, physical, temporal, functional, social and modality context).
numbers: Abstract only: 9 dimensions; number of studies reviewed not stated on the page.
limits: Only the PubMed abstract was read, not the full paper. The dimension names are from background knowledge, not this page.
agent_relevance: Tag each lesson-transfer test by domain, format, time gap and modality. Report per cell, not one headline number.

source: Singley and Anderson (1989) The transfer of cognitive skill
finding: Formal identical-elements model. Production rules are the elements. Transfer tracks the number of shared productions, including between text editors. Also predicts, and finds, no transfer between skills that share little.
numbers: Line-editor experience to EMACS: about 46% transfer for the move-type component vs 102% between ED and EDT; line-locating component 89%. Prior line editing saved about 35 seconds per edit on EMACS day 1, under half the savings among line-editor users. Calculus: no transfer among translating word problems, choosing operators and applying them.
limits: Lab studies of a few skills. Total encapsulation was too strong because productions share a declarative base.
agent_relevance: Near transfer is predictable from overlap in procedures. For the agent, measure overlap in steps or operators before expecting a lesson to carry.

source: Singley and Anderson (1989) The transfer of cognitive skill (Thorndike 1922 data)
finding: Thorndike's own test of changed data: skilled algebra subjects solved about half of the exercises with novel forms. The strong surface-identity version is not supported.
numbers: About 50% correct on novel exercises; in one of six exercises performance was not damaged.
limits: Secondhand description of Thorndike (1922). The original was not opened.
agent_relevance: Surface identity is not required; some structure carries. Surface change still costs accuracy.

source: Trninic, Kapur and Sinha (2020) The disappearing advantage of abstract examples in learning mathematics (critical replication of Kaminski et al. 2008)
finding: Original claim: abstract training transfers better than concrete. Original: transfer 76% abstract vs 44% concrete (n=18 and 20), d above 1.6, equal learning. A replication with improved concrete examples found no abstract advantage.
numbers: 114 recruited, 38 per condition. Initial learning: concrete 95% vs abstract 70% (d=1.276, p<.001). Abstract transfer: no difference (d=-0.176, p=.835). Concrete transfer: concrete better (d=0.416, p=.033).
quote: the previously reported 'advantage of abstract examples' manifested not because abstract examples are advantageous in general
limits: Original table cells read from a garbled text extraction. The replicating team argues against the original on design grounds.
agent_relevance: Good concrete worked cases can match abstract rules. Lesson reuse should not rely on abstraction alone; the quality of stored examples matters.

source: De Bock, Deprez, Van Dooren, Roelens and Verschaffel (2011) Abstract or concrete examples in learning mathematics? A replication and elaboration of Kaminski, Sloutsky and Heckler
finding: Replicated the abstract advantage for transfer to an abstract domain, but concrete training was better for transfer to a concrete domain. Transfer follows the match between learning format and target format.
numbers: Belgian undergraduates in four conditions: AA n=23, AC n=30, CA n=28, CC n=24 (conditions as described in the Trninic review; cell scores not read cleanly).
limits: Read only via the Trninic et al. summary, not the original paper. Participants removed in two elimination steps as in the original.
agent_relevance: Where a lesson was learned and where it is used should match, or be bridged. Store lessons with format tags.

source: Loewenstein, Thompson and Gentner (2003) Analogical learning in negotiation teams: comparing cases promotes learning and transfer
finding: Comparing two cases beats studying them separately for transfer to a new face-to-face negotiation, in MBA students.
numbers: Contingent contracts formed: Comparison 24/60 (40%), Separate cases 8/37 (22%), Baseline 50/213 (23%); chi-square(2, N=310)=7.08, p<.05. Schema induced: 21/38 (55%) vs 12/38 (32%), chi-square 4.34, p<.05. Groups with contingent contracts: expected joint gain $5.33M vs $4.12M.
limits: One task type (negotiation); teams and solo participants pooled. Comparison vs separate cases was only marginal (p=.06).
agent_relevance: Best applied evidence for compare two cases then abstract. A direct template for lesson formation in O7.

source: Sourati, Ilievski, Sommerauer and Jiang (2024) ARN: Analogical Reasoning on Narratives
finding: LLMs match humans on near analogies but collapse on far analogies (no surface overlap). The same near/far split as in human transfer.
numbers: Zero-shot, chance 50%. Humans 96.0% average; models average 57.3%. Near analogy: humans 97.9% vs models 75.0%. Far analogy: humans 94.1% vs models 39.6% (below chance). GPT-4 close to humans on near, below random on far. (Far, far) 45.3%; far analogy against near distractor 33.9%; SBERT 1% on that partition.
limits: 1.1k triples of proverb-based narratives; six LLMs from 2023 and 2024 (GPT-4, GPT-3.5, Llama-2, Flan-T5, UnifiedQA, Macaw).
agent_relevance: Surface-similarity retrieval is a trap for lesson reuse: a near-but-wrong lesson beats a far-but-right one, as in Gick and Holyoak.

source: Sourati, Ilievski, Sommerauer and Jiang (2024) ARN: Analogical Reasoning on Narratives (few-shot)
finding: Solved demonstrations help far analogies but hurt near ones. Models do not use demonstrations efficiently.
numbers: GPT-3.5 and Llama-2 gained close to 10 absolute points on far analogies with demonstrations and lost much of their near-analogy performance. GPT-4 was most stable: far slightly up, near slightly down. Best few-shot model still only halfway between random and human.
limits: Random demonstrations, three runs averaged. Chain-of-thought gains are stated in the abstract but their numbers were not extracted.
agent_relevance: Examples can shift the model toward far matches at the cost of near ones. Choose and order lesson examples on purpose.

source: Webb, Holyoak and Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: GPT-3 matches or beats UCLA undergraduates on several text analogy tasks. In a Gick and Holyoak style test it solves the radiation problem after the general story, and fails again when distractor stories are added until told to consider earlier stories.
numbers: Digit Matrices, humans N=40: GPT-3 better, OR=1.88 [1.21,2.91] (generative), 6.27 (multiple choice). Letter-string, N=57: OR=1.76 [1.34,2.31]. Story analogies, N=54: humans better, OR=0.37 [0.21,0.63]; GPT-4 stronger. Radiation problem alone: non-convergence answer. With general story: convergence. With two distractor stories: fails. With a prompt to consider the earlier stories: succeeds.
limits: Radiation test was qualitative (single prompts, no rate). Training-data exposure is not ruled out; see counterfactual tests.
agent_relevance: The LLM shows the same noticing failure as people and the same fix: an explicit prompt to check earlier items. Build that prompt into O7.

source: Lewis and Mitchell (2024) Using counterfactual tasks to evaluate the generality of analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: On letter-string analogies with unusual alphabets, human accuracy stays high but GPT models drop sharply. Evidence against general abstract transfer.
numbers: Humans: 136 recruited. Pooled letter-string accuracy: humans 0.753 [0.734,0.773] (1,876 samples), GPT-3 0.488, GPT-3.5 0.350, GPT-4 0.452 (6,840 samples each). Per-condition (original vs counterfactual) values are only in a figure and were not read.
limits: Pooled table only. Models are 2023 era.
agent_relevance: Models solve familiar forms and fail on rare forms with the same logic. In-distribution analogy success is weak evidence of far transfer.

source: Letter-string analogy generalization in children, adults and LLMs: Can large language models generalize analogy solving like children can? (arXiv 2411.02348, TACL)
finding: Children and adults carry a rule to unfamiliar alphabets. LLMs lose accuracy as the alphabet gets less familiar. The near-to-far slope is steep for models and flat for people.
numbers: Proportion correct (Latin, Greek near, symbol far): adults 0.88/0.91/0.89 (N=62); children 0.62/0.66/0.67 (N=42, ages 7 to 9); GPT-4o 0.85/0.63/0.48; Claude-3.5 0.68/0.62/0.46; Llama-3.1 405B 0.79/0.74/0.27; Gemma-2 27B 0.60/0.39/0.14. Prompt template changed total means from 0.52 to 0.74.
limits: About 54 runs per model. Chain-of-thought not tested. Author names not read from the fetched text.
agent_relevance: Models that look strong at baseline lose about half of their accuracy on the far form. Include far-form tests for any lesson mechanism.

source: Yasunaga et al. (2023) Large language models as analogical reasoners
finding: Having the model write its own relevant examples before solving gives modest gains over 0-shot and few-shot chain-of-thought.
numbers: GSM8K: GPT-3.5-turbo 75.8 (0-shot CoT), 76.7 (5-shot CoT), 77.8 (analogical); PaLM 2 78.2, 80.7, 81.7; text-davinci-003 50.3, 54.0, 61.0. MATH: GPT-3.5 33.9, 34.9, 37.3. Codeforces GPT-4 Acc@1 16%, 17%, 19%. BIG-Bench word sorting 67.6 to 75.2. Average gain about +4 points.
limits: Codeforces set only 50 problems. Gains small on strong models. Needs a strong model, more output tokens, prompt sensitive.
agent_relevance: Recall-your-own-analogs is a cheap form of O7. Gains are small, so test it per model strength.

source: ExpeL: LLM agents are experiential learners (2023)
finding: An agent that extracts natural-language insights from past tasks beats ReAct and matches Reflexion. Insights carry to a related task.
numbers: gpt-3.5-turbo: ALFWorld ReAct 40.0, Reflexion 54.4 (R3), ExpeL 59.0. HotpotQA ReAct 28.0, Reflexion 39, ExpeL 39.0. Transfer HotpotQA to FEVER: Act 58, ReAct 63, ExpeL transfer without task demos 65, ExpeL transfer 70.
limits: Source and target are similar question-answering tasks (near transfer). Paper text and table disagree slightly on some figures. Author names not read.
agent_relevance: Real lesson reuse on a near task gave +7 points over ReAct on FEVER. Far-class transfer is untested here.

source: Does math reasoning improve general LLM capabilities? Understanding transferability of LLM reasoning (2025)
finding: Math training mostly fails to transfer to non-math domains when done by supervised fine-tuning. Reinforcement learning transfers. SFT harms other abilities.
numbers: 20+ open-weight reasoning models. Controlled study Qwen3-14B-Base on 47K math problems: other-reasoning average 30.2 base, 45.3 SFT-think, 60.0 RL. Non-reasoning average 45.7 base, 21.1 SFT-think, 29.0 SFT-no-think, 53.2 RL. Transfer index for non-reasoning: SFT -104.1 and -278.9, RL +52.2.
limits: Weight training, not prompt scaffolds. Open-weight models only. Author names not read.
agent_relevance: Same pattern as human far transfer: narrow practice does not spread and the learning method matters. A scaffold-only agent should expect lessons to carry only where structure is shared.

source: Sala, Aksayli, Tatlidil, Tatsumi, Gondo and Gobet (2019) Near and far transfer in cognitive training: a second-order meta-analysis
finding: Meta-analysis of meta-analyses. Near transfer exists. Far transfer is small or null whatever the program or population.
numbers: From search summaries only: data set covers 332 studies and 1,555 effect sizes. Preprint averages reported as near g about 0.27 and far g about 0.12. A reanalysis of a Melby-Lervag subsample gave near 0.37 and far 0.02.
limits: Not opened: full text was blocked. Numbers come from search summaries.
agent_relevance: Supports expecting near transfer only as the default.

source: Detterman (1993) The case for the prosecution: transfer as an epiphenomenon
finding: Skeptic's view that transfer is rare and weak unless situations are nearly identical.
numbers: Not extracted.
limits: Not opened. Only seen as a search hit and the DTIC link was not confirmed as this chapter.
agent_relevance: Follow-up item for the sceptic side of the debate.

source: Lewis and Mitchell (2024) and ARN together: surface cues versus structure
finding: Surface mappings are the strongest distractors for models in ARN; GPT-4 and the model average were most distracted by action-based surface mappings.
numbers: ARN distractor ablation: action-based surface mappings gave the strongest distraction for GPT-4 and most models; the aggregate of all surface mappings distracted more than any single element.
limits: Distractor analysis was run on the two best models and read from the paper text.
agent_relevance: When fetching lessons, filter surface matches by structure. Keep structure cues (goal, constraint, failure type) in the lesson index.
